(3) Nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped, (4) nor are you worshipers of what I worship. (5) For you is your religion, and for me is my religion.﴾ [al-Kafirun 1–6].

This surah is one of the two surahs of Sincerity (al-Ikhlas), for the two surahs of Sincerity are: "Say: O you disbelievers" and "Say: He is Allah, the One" (Surat al-Ikhlas). "The Prophet ﷺ used to recite them both in the two Sunnah prayers of Fajr, in the two Sunnah prayers of Maghrib, and in the two rak'ahs of Tawaf"[[Ahmad (5215) narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited in the two rak'ahs before Fajr and the two rak'ahs after Maghrib, some twenty or about ten times: "Say: O you disbelievers" and "Say: He is Allah, the One." Muslim (1218/147) also narrated, from the long hadith of Jabir concerning Hajj, that the Prophet ﷺ used to recite in the two rak'ahs "Say: He is Allah, the One" and "Say: O you disbelievers."]]; because of what they contain of sincerity to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and praise of Him with His perfect attributes, found in the surah "Say: He is Allah, the One."

Allah says, commanding His Prophet: ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, he calls them, declares to them by calling: ﴿O you disbelievers﴾, and this includes every disbeliever, whether from the polytheists, or from the Jews, or from the Christians, or from the Communists, or from others; every disbeliever you must address, with your heart or your tongue if he is present, so that you disassociate yourself from him and from his worship.

﴿Say: O you disbelievers (1) I do not worship what you worship (2) nor are you worshipers of what I worship (3) nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped (4) nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ The sentences are repeated two by two.

﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ meaning: I do not worship those whom you worship, namely the idols.

﴿Nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ namely Allah. And ﴿mā﴾ here in His saying ﴿what I worship﴾ means (man) "who", because when the relative pronoun refers to Allah, it comes in the form (man).

﴿I do not worship what you worship (2) nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ meaning: I do not worship your idols, and you do not worship Allah.

﴿Nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped (4) nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ Now, one may think that these are repeated for emphasis, but that is not so, because the form is different. ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ — is this a verb or a noun? A question.

* The students: A verb.

* The Shaykh: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ is a verb. ﴿Nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped (4) nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ — ﴿worshiper (ʿābid)﴾ and ﴿worshipers (ʿābidūn)﴾?

* Students: Nouns.

* The Shaykh: Nouns. Emphasis requires that the second sentence be like the first, so the claim that it is repeated for emphasis is weak. So why this repetition?

Some scholars said: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ now, and ﴿nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped﴾ in the future. This is one view. So ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ means what? In the present; ﴿nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped﴾ means in the future, because the present-tense verb indicates the present, and the active participle indicates the future, as evidenced by its governing an object, and the active participle does not govern except when it refers to the future.

So ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ refers to the present, and ﴿nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped﴾ ... ﴿Say: O you disbelievers (1) I do not worship what you worship﴾ now, ﴿nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ meaning now, ﴿nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped﴾ meaning in the future, ﴿nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ meaning in the future.

But an objection is raised against this view: how does He say ﴿nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ when they may believe and then worship Allah? According to this view, there is some weakness in it.

They answered that His saying ﴿nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ addresses the polytheists whom Allah, Exalted, knew would never believe, so the address is not general; and this somewhat weakens the view. So we now have two views: the first, that it is emphasis; the second, that it refers to the future.

The third view: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ means I do not worship the idols that you worship, ﴿nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ means you do not worship Allah, ﴿nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped (4) nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ means in the manner of worship: my worship is not like your worship, nor is your worship like my worship. So this is a negation of the act, not of the object of worship; that is, it is not a negation of the one worshipped, but a negation of the worship: I do not worship as you worship, nor do you worship as I worship, because my worship is sincerely for Allah, and your worship is the worship of shirk.

How many views are there now? Three.

The fourth view, chosen by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him: that His saying ﴿I do not worship what you worship (2) nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ refers to the act, agreeing with the first view for this sentence, while ﴿nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped (4) nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾ means in acceptance; that is: I will not accept other than my worship, and I will not accept your worship, and you likewise will not accept. So the first sentence refers to the act, and the second sentence refers to acceptance and approval; that is: I do not worship Him and I do not approve of it, and you likewise do not worship Allah nor approve of His worship. If you reflect on this view, no objection from the previous ones (...) applies to it, so it is a good and sound view.

From here we learn that the Noble Qur'an contains nothing repeated without benefit at all; there is nothing repeated except that it has a purpose, because if we said that the Qur'an contains something repeated without benefit, there would be in the Qur'an something vain, and it is free of that. On this basis, the repetition in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman 13] and in Surat al-Mursalat: ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat 15] is not without benefit; rather it is a repetition for a great benefit, namely that every verse between these repeated verses contains great blessings and magnificent favors. Moreover, there is a verbal benefit in it: alerting the addressee, since it is repeated to him: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ and it is repeated to him: ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾. "For you is your religion": the religion you are upon and follow. "And for me is my religion": so I am free of your religion, and you are free of my religion.

Some of the scholars said: this surah was revealed before the obligation of jihad, because after jihad, the disbeliever is not allowed to remain upon his religion except by paying the jizya if he is from the People of the Book, and according to the preponderant opinion, or from others as well.

However, the correct view is that it does not contradict the command to fight, so that we would say it has been abrogated (mansukh). Rather, it remains in force, and it is obligatory for us to disavow the religion of the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists at all times and in all circumstances. For this reason we allow the Jews and Christians to remain upon their religion in return for the jizya, while we worship Allah and they worship what they worship.

In any case, this surah contains the disavowal and renunciation of worshipping other than Allah the Mighty and Majestic, whether in the object worshipped or in the type of act. It also contains sincerity to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and that we worship none but Allah alone, without partner.

Here ends what was made possible of discussion on this surah.
